See: [Matematica: Calcolo infinitesimale: Integrali](https://basics2022.github.io/bbooks-math-miscellanea-hs/ch/infinitesimal_calculus/integrals.html)

*Definite integrals* are first introduced with its geometrical interpretation. The formal definition as the limit of a Riemann sum follows. **Fundamental theorem of calculus** provides the relation between integral and derivative.

## Geometrical Interpretation

The value of the *definite* integral 

$$\int_{x=a}^{b} f(x) \, dx \ ,$$

equals the area (with sign) in the Cartesian plane between the $x$-axis and the graph of the function $y = f(x)$, and the vertical lines with coordinates $x = a$, and $x = b$. This value can be approximated with the sum of the area of rectangles or trapezoids (see APPROXIMATION RULEs): as the number of the elementary geometrical shapes of the approximation increases, and their height (in $x$ direction) decreases, the approaximation becomes better and better. As the number of elements goes to $\infty$, and the maximum height of the elementary shapes goes to zero, the definition of the definite Riemann integral follows

$$\int_{x=a}^{b} f(x) \, dx = \lim_{\max h_k \rightarrow 0} \sum_{k} \text{Area}_k \ .$$

If this limit exists, then the integral of the function $f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ exists. This definition is independent from the approximation (as long as it's a definite approximation...): you can easily check that the value of the *Riemann Sum Approximation* tends to the value of the *Exact Definite Integral*, while the absolute error and the relative error percentage go to zero.
